lessons.title: Lesson 1: The kinds of farm risk and a risk register
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List your farm's main risks and rank them in a simple risk register.
This lesson builds toward: Thinking about your own farm and household, you will list the main risks you face and rank them in a risk register by how likely they are and how much damage they would do, with at least one risk of each kind (production, market, money, rules and people) and one action for each of the top five.
Farm risks come in five kinds. Production risks: drought, floods, pests such as fall armyworm, diseases in crops and animals, theft. Market risks: prices falling, buyers not paying or not collecting, input prices rising. Money risks: debt you cannot repay, loss of savings, inflation, exchange rates for exports such as coffee and cocoa. Rule risks: new taxes, export bans, changes in land or market rules. People risks: illness, injury or death in the family, or losing a key worker.
A risk register is a table with one line per risk. For each one, score how likely it is (1 low, 2 medium, 3 high) and how much damage it would do (1 small, 2 medium, 3 large). Multiply the two to get a score from 1 to 9. The highest scores come first.
For each top risk, choose an action: avoid it (do not plant tomatoes in the wettest month), reduce it (drought-tolerant seed, vaccines as the vet advises, storage), share or move it (insurance, a contract, a cooperative), or accept it and keep savings for it. Review the register before each season.
Step by step:
- List risks of each kind: production, market, money, rules, people.
- Score how likely each is: 1, 2 or 3.
- Score the damage each would do: 1, 2 or 3.
- Multiply the scores and rank the risks.
- For the top five, choose avoid, reduce, share or accept, and one action.
- Review before every season.
Words to know:
- Risk: something that may happen and would harm your farm or income.
- Risk register: a table listing your risks, how likely and how harmful each is, and what you will do.
- Likelihood: how probable it is that something will happen.
- Impact: how much damage it would do if it happened.
Try it now: Write a risk register for your farm with at least eight risks covering all five kinds. Score each one, rank them, and write an avoid, reduce, share or accept action for the top five.
You can now list your farm's risks, rank them and choose an action for the most serious ones.

check.q: Maize prices fall by half at harvest. What kind of risk is this?
A risk has likelihood 3 and impact 2. What is its score?

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Price swings and reading market trends
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Keep a weekly price log from at least two sources and describe the trend.
This lesson builds toward: For your main crop or animal, over four weeks, you will record prices weekly from at least two sources, including an official market information service where one exists, and describe the trend, with the same product, grade and unit each week.
Prices for crops and animals rise and fall with the season, the weather, imports and exports, fuel costs and demand. Many staple prices are lowest at harvest, when everyone sells, and higher in the months before the next harvest. Even a price set by government can change a lot between seasons: in Cote d'Ivoire, the guaranteed farmgate price for cocoa was 2,800 CFA francs per kg in the 2025-2026 main season, and the government set it at 1,200 per kg for the intermediate season from March 2026, after world cocoa prices fell.
Use official market information services where they exist. In Kenya, the Ministry of Agriculture's KAMIS publishes market prices. In Nigeria, the National Bureau of Statistics publishes a monthly food price report by state. In Ghana, the Ghana Commodity Exchange publishes the prices of its trades. Add radio market reports, your cooperative and at least two buyers.
Keep a price log: each week, the date, the market or source, the product, grade and unit (for example a 90 kg bag of dry maize), and the price. After four weeks or more, look at the direction: rising, falling or flat. Compare with the same months last year if you can. A trend is a guide, not a promise: prices can turn quickly.
Step by step:
- Choose your main product, grade and unit.
- Pick at least two sources, including an official service where one exists.
- Each week write: date, source, product, grade, unit, price.
- After four weeks, mark the direction: rising, falling or flat.
- Compare with the same months last year.
- Share the log with your group.
Words to know:
- Market information service: a service that collects and shares prices from markets, by website, SMS or radio.
- Trend: the general direction prices are moving over several weeks or months.
- Farmgate price: the price paid to the farmer at the farm, before transport to market.
Official sources:
- Kenya Agricultural Market Information System (KAMIS), Ministry of Agriculture: market prices
- National Bureau of Statistics, Nigeria (monthly Selected Food Prices Watch and inflation)
- Ghana Commodity Exchange (GCX), official site
- Financial Afrik (5 March 2026): Cote d'Ivoire sets the intermediate-season cocoa farmgate price at 1,200 FCFA/kg
Try it now: Start a price log for your main crop or animal today. Write this week's price from two sources, with product, grade and unit, and set a reminder on your phone for the same day each week.
You can now keep a weekly price log from official and local sources and describe the price trend.

check.q: Why write the grade and unit with every price in your log?
options: So you compare the same thing each week
check.why: A price for a 50 kg bag of wet maize cannot be compared with a 90 kg bag of dry maize.

check.q: Over five weeks, a market's tomato price went 400, 420, 450, 470, 500 per crate. What is the trend?
check.why: Each week the price is higher than the week before.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Spreading risk: diversification, staged selling and storage
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate whether storing pays and write a plan to sell in stages.
This lesson builds toward: Given a harvest, today's price, an expected later price and storage costs, you will calculate the storage break-even price and write a plan to sell in stages and spread risk, with correct numbers and cash needs at harvest covered.
Diversification means not putting everything in one basket: two or more crops with different seasons or markets, a few goats or chickens, fish, trees, or off-farm income. When one fails, another may still pay. Do not spread so thin that you cannot manage any of them well.
Staged selling means selling part of the harvest at different times instead of all at once. For example, sell a third at harvest to cover school fees and debts, a third two months later and a third four months later. You avoid selling everything at the lowest price, and you avoid betting everything on a high price that may not come.
Storage only pays if the later price covers the storage costs and losses. Storage break-even price = (harvest price x bags + storage costs) / bags you will sell later. Example (made-up numbers in Kenya shillings): 10 bags of maize, harvest price 3,000 a bag, storage costs 3,000 for four months (hermetic bags, store, checks). Break-even = (30,000 + 3,000) / 10 = 3,300 a bag. If the price reaches 4,200 you gain; if it only reaches 3,200 you lose. Store only clean, dry grain in hermetic bags or a certified warehouse, and check it for pests and mould.
Step by step:
- List what else you could grow, keep or earn so one failure does not ruin you.
- Work out how much cash you need at harvest.
- Plan to sell enough at harvest for that cash, and store the rest in stages.
- Storage break-even = (harvest price x bags + storage costs) / bags.
- Compare it with the price trend in your log.
- Store only clean, dry produce safely, and check it.
Words to know:
- Diversification: spreading your farming and income across several activities so one failure does not ruin you.
- Staged selling: selling a harvest in parts at different times instead of all at once.
- Storage break-even price: the later price you need to cover the harvest price you gave up plus storage costs.
- Hermetic bag: an airtight storage bag that stops insects breathing, so stored grain stays safe without chemicals.
Official sources:
- Purdue University: Purdue Improved Crop Storage (PICS) hermetic bags
Try it now: For your main crop, write how many bags or kg you expect, how much cash you need at harvest, and how much you will sell at harvest, after two months and after four months. Work out the storage break-even price for the part you will store.
You can now work out whether storage pays, plan to sell in stages and spread risk across more than one activity.

check.q: Harvest price 5,000 a bag, 20 bags, storage costs 10,000. What is the storage break-even price?
What is the main benefit of selling in stages?
options: You avoid selling everything at the lowest price or betting it all on a high price
Buyers always pay more for small amounts
check.why: Selling in parts spreads the price risk over several dates.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Fixed-price contracts, hedging and commodity exchanges
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: List the terms to check in a fixed-price contract and explain what hedging means.
This lesson builds toward: Given a forward or fixed-price contract offer, you will list the terms to check and explain what you gain and what you give up, including how hedging on a commodity exchange works, naming at least five terms and both a gain and a risk.
A forward or fixed-price contract is an agreement now to sell a set amount and quality at a set price on a later date. You gain certainty: you know your price before harvest, which helps you plan and borrow. You give something up: if the market price rises, you still get the agreed price. If your harvest fails or you sell elsewhere (side-selling), you may break the contract and owe a penalty. Before signing, check: product and grade, quantity, price or how it is set, delivery date and place, who pays transport, quality tests and rejection, payment date and method, and what happens if the harvest fails or the buyer does not collect.
Hedging means taking a position that gains when your crop loses value, so the two balance out. On a commodity exchange, large traders and processors do this with futures: standard contracts to buy or sell later at a price agreed today. If prices fall, the futures position gains while the crop earns less; if prices rise, the futures position loses while the crop earns more. It needs a broker, deposits called margin that can be called at short notice, and skill. It can lose money and is not something to try without training and advice.
In Africa, the Nigeria Commodity Exchange (NCX) is licensed by Nigeria's Securities and Exchange Commission and offers trade, price discovery, storage and grading of commodities. The Ghana Commodity Exchange (GCX), regulated by Ghana's Securities and Exchange Commission, began electronic spot trading of maize in 2018 and links farmers to certified warehouses. Most smallholders reach exchanges through a cooperative, aggregator or certified warehouse, not by trading themselves. This course does not recommend trading. Anyone promising you profits from commodity trading may be a scammer: check with the securities regulator.
Step by step:
- Read the whole contract, aloud with your group if possible.
- Check product, grade, quantity, price, delivery date and place, and transport.
- Check quality tests, rejection, payment date and method.
- Ask what happens if the harvest fails or the buyer does not collect.
- Compare the fixed price with your break-even price and price log.
- Ask your cooperative, extension officer or a lawyer before signing.
Words to know:
- Forward contract: an agreement now to sell a set amount at a set price on a later date.
- Hedging: taking a position that gains when your crop loses value, so the losses balance out.
- Futures: standard contracts traded on an exchange to buy or sell a commodity later at a price agreed now.
- Commodity exchange: a regulated market where buyers and sellers trade crops and other goods by agreed grades and rules.
- Side-selling: selling produce promised to one buyer to someone else.
Official sources:
- Nigeria Commodity Exchange (NCX): about us (licensed by the Securities and Exchange Commission)
- Ghana Commodity Exchange (GCX), official site
- MyJoyOnline: Ghana Commodity Exchange executes first electronic trade (maize spot contracts, 2018)
Try it now: Take a real or example buyer contract. Write each of the eight terms from the steps and what the contract says (or "missing"). Then write one thing you gain and one risk you take if you sign it.
You can now check a fixed-price contract term by term and explain what hedging on a commodity exchange means and why it carries risk.

check.q: You sign a fixed price of 30,000 a bag. At delivery, the market price is 36,000. What do you get?
check.why: A fixed-price contract pays the agreed price even if the market rises.

check.q: A stranger offers to trade commodity futures for you with "guaranteed profits". What should you do?
options: Refuse and check the company with the securities regulator
Send a small deposit to test it
Give your mobile money PIN so they can trade
Sign quickly before the offer ends
check.why: No one can guarantee trading profits; it is a sign of a scam.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Index-based crop and livestock insurance
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check an index insurance offer for its index, trigger, premium, basis risk and licence.
This lesson builds toward: Given an index-based crop or livestock insurance offer, you will check the index, the trigger, the premium, the basis risk and the insurer's licence, before you pay, writing down the answer to each.
Ordinary insurance sends someone to measure the loss on your farm. Index insurance pays when an index crosses a set level, called the trigger: for example rainfall measured by satellite or a weather station falling below normal, the average yield in your area falling, or satellite pictures showing pasture drying up. Nobody visits your field, so it can be cheaper and pay faster.
Examples: ACRE Africa, an authorized insurance intermediary based in Kenya, works with local insurers to offer weather index, area yield index and index-based livestock insurance, often sold through farmer groups and paid by mobile money. Kenya's government runs the Kenya Livestock Insurance Programme (KLIP), launched in 2015 using index-based livestock insurance developed with ILRI: the government pays the premium for registered vulnerable pastoralists, and payouts are triggered when satellite pictures show pasture failing, so herders get cash to keep animals alive. In Senegal, the national agricultural insurance company CNAAS insures crops and livestock and offers index insurance.
The big weakness is basis risk: the index may not match your own field. Your crop can fail from a local hailstorm while the area's rainfall looks normal, so no payout comes, or the index can trigger when your field did well. Before you pay, ask: what risk is covered, what index and where is it measured, what is the trigger, how much is the payout, what is the premium and the deadline to buy, how and when it pays, and is the insurer licensed (Kenya: Insurance Regulatory Authority; Nigeria: NAICOM; Ghana: National Insurance Commission; CFA franc countries: CIMA and the national insurance office).
Step by step:
- Ask what risk is covered: drought, excess rain, area yield loss or pasture failure.
- Ask what the index is and where it is measured.
- Ask the trigger and the payout amount.
- Ask the premium, the deadline to buy and how payouts reach you.
- Think about basis risk: would the index match your field?
- Check the insurer or agent is licensed by the insurance regulator.
Words to know:
- Index insurance: insurance that pays when a measured index, such as rainfall or pasture, crosses a set level, not on a visit to your farm.
- Trigger: the index level that makes the insurer pay.
- Premium: the price you pay for insurance cover.
- Basis risk: the chance that the index does not match what really happened on your farm.
Official sources:
- ACRE Africa: weather index insurance (an authorized insurance intermediary)
- ILRI: Index-Based Livestock Insurance (IBLI) and the Kenya Livestock Insurance Programme (KLIP)
- ILRI: Eyes in the sky: Kenya's government provides pastoralists with livestock insurance through satellite imagery
- CNAAS, Compagnie Nationale d'Assurance Agricole du Senegal
Try it now: Ask your cooperative, input dealer or extension officer about one index insurance product near you (or use an example). Write the answers to the eight questions in the steps, and write one way basis risk could affect your farm.
You can now check an index insurance offer for its index, trigger, premium, basis risk and licence before you pay.

check.q: What makes an index insurance policy pay out?
options: The index crossing the trigger level
check.why: Index insurance pays on the measured index, not on a field visit.

check.q: Your maize was destroyed by a local hailstorm, but the area rainfall index stayed normal. What is this called?
check.why: Basis risk is when the index does not match what happened on your farm.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Inflation and keeping your savings
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Compare ways to keep savings and choose a mix that protects them from inflation and theft.
This lesson builds toward: Given your savings and the current inflation rate, you will compare at least three ways to keep savings and choose a mix that protects them from inflation and theft, naming a risk for each way and checking any SACCO, bank or microfinance institution is licensed.
Inflation means prices in general are rising, so the same money buys less. Example: if prices rise 10% in a year, 10,000 kept in a tin at home will buy only what about 9,100 buys today. Find the current inflation rate from your central bank or statistics office (Kenya: Central Bank of Kenya; Nigeria: National Bureau of Statistics; CFA franc countries in West Africa: BCEAO).
Each way of saving has a risk. Cash at home: easy to reach, but loses value to inflation and can be stolen. A savings group or VSLA: builds a habit and may pay a share-out, but depends on honest records. A licensed SACCO, bank or microfinance account: safer and may pay interest, but compare the interest with inflation and check fees. Livestock: can grow in value, but can die of drought or disease. Stored grain: may rise in price, but can spoil or fall in price. Buying key inputs early: avoids price rises, but needs safe storage.
Spread your savings across more than one way. Keep an emergency fund you can reach quickly. Check that any SACCO, bank or microfinance institution is licensed (in Kenya, SASRA lists licensed deposit-taking SACCOs). Be very careful with any scheme that promises high, fast returns: it is often a fraud. This lesson explains how saving works; it is not investment advice. Ask a trusted adviser for your own situation.
Step by step:
- Find the current inflation rate from your central bank or statistics office.
- List where your savings are now: cash, group, SACCO, bank, animals, grain.
- Write one risk for each.
- Choose a mix of at least three, with an emergency fund you can reach fast.
- Check every SACCO, bank or microfinance institution is licensed.
- Refuse schemes that promise high, fast returns.
Words to know:
- Inflation: a general rise in prices, so the same money buys less.
- Interest: money a bank or SACCO pays you for keeping your savings, or that you pay to borrow.
- Emergency fund: savings kept for sudden problems, such as illness or a failed harvest, that you can reach quickly.
- VSLA: village savings and loan association: a group that saves together, lends to members and shares out the savings and profits.
Official sources:
- Central Bank of Kenya (inflation and licensed institutions)
- National Bureau of Statistics, Nigeria (monthly Selected Food Prices Watch and inflation)
- BCEAO, Central Bank of West African States: main indicators, including inflation
- SASRA, Kenya: list of licensed deposit-taking SACCOs
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page farm risk plan: top five risks with actions, a four-week price log and its trend, your selling and storage plan with the storage break-even price, your questions for a contract and for index insurance, and your savings mix against inflation.
You can now protect your savings from inflation with a licensed, spread-out mix and bring all your risk tools together in one plan.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Risk register Fewer than five risks, or risks are not scored or have no actions. At least eight risks covering all five kinds, scored and ranked, with an action for each of the top five. Actions have dates and costs, and the plan says when the register will be reviewed. Price log and trend Fewer than four weeks, one source only, or units and grades mixed. Four weeks from at least two sources, same product, grade and unit, with the trend described. Includes an official service and the same months last year, and says what the trend means for selling. Selling and storage plan No storage break-even price, or cash needs at harvest are ignored. Correct storage break-even price, cash needs covered at harvest, and sales planned in stages. Also adds a second enterprise or market to spread risk, and safe storage steps. Contract and insurance questions Fewer than five contract terms, or no insurance questions. At least eight contract terms with a gain and a risk, and what hedging means in one sentence. Compares the fixed price with the break-even price and price log. Index insurance check Index, trigger, premium or basis risk is missing. Index, trigger, payout, premium, deadline, basis risk and licence check are all answered. Answers come from a real offer near the farm, with the regulator named. Savings against inflation One way of saving only, or no risks named. At least three ways compared, each with a risk, the inflation rate noted and licences checked. Includes an emergency fund amount and a date to review the mix. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the plan and check it again.

check.q: Prices rose 10% this year. What happened to 10,000 kept in a tin at home?
options: It buys less than it did a year ago
check.why: The same money buys less when prices rise.

check.q: A group promises to double your savings in three months. What does this most likely show?
options: A likely fraud: high, fast returns are a warning sign
check.why: Promises of high, fast returns are a common sign of fraud.
